reading.title: Attention Is All You Need

summary.beginner: Computers used to translate sentences one word at a time, like reading with a finger under each word. This paper shows a new design, the **Transformer**, that looks at every word at once and lets each word decide which other words matter to it. It translated better than anything before it and trained much faster, and it later became the base of chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude.
summary.student: The paper introduces the **Transformer**, a sequence-to-sequence model built only from attention layers, with no recurrence (RNNs) and no convolutions. Because every position is processed in parallel, it trains far faster on GPUs, and it set new records on English-to-German (28.4 BLEU) and English-to-French (41.8 BLEU) translation.
summary.expert: An encoder-decoder architecture that replaces recurrent and convolutional layers entirely with multi-head scaled dot-product self-attention plus position-wise feed-forward layers and sinusoidal positional encodings. It reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT14 En-De (+2 over prior ensembles) and 41.8 BLEU single-model on WMT14 En-Fr after 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs, at a fraction of prior training cost.

contributions: A translation model built entirely from attention, with no recurrent or convolutional layers.
Multi-head attention: several attention operations run side by side, each free to focus on different relationships.
Sinusoidal positional encodings that tell an order-blind model where each word sits.
New state-of-the-art translation scores at a small fraction of the previous training cost.

prerequisites.primer: A vector is a list of numbers, and a matrix is a table of them. Multiplying a matrix by a vector mixes the numbers into a new list, and that is how neural networks turn one representation into another.
prerequisites.why: Every word becomes a vector, and queries, keys and values are made by matrix multiplication.

prerequisites.primer: The dot product multiplies two lists number by number and adds the results. It is large when the two lists point the same way, so it works as a similarity score.
prerequisites.why: Attention scores how well a query matches each key with a dot product.

prerequisites.primer: Softmax turns a list of any numbers into positive weights that add up to 1, giving the largest numbers most of the weight.
prerequisites.why: The match scores go through a softmax to become attention weights.

prerequisites.primer: A neural network is layers of matrix multiplications with simple bends (like ReLU) between them, tuned by gradient descent to reduce its mistakes.
prerequisites.why: The Transformer is built from these layers, plus residual connections and layer normalization.

prerequisites.primer: An embedding gives each word a learned vector, so words used in similar ways get similar vectors.
prerequisites.why: The model's input and output are word embeddings, with position information added.

prerequisites.primer: An RNN reads a sentence one word at a time, carrying a memory forward. That makes it slow to train, because each step waits for the one before.
prerequisites.why: The paper's main argument is that attention can replace recurrence and train much faster.

explanation.beginner:
Before this paper, the best translation programs read a sentence one word after another, carrying a running memory forward. That is slow, because word 10 has to wait for word 9, and the memory of early words fades by the end of a long sentence.

The authors ask a bold question: what if the model skipped the step-by-step reading and simply let every word look directly at every other word? That idea, called **attention**, had already been used as a helper. Here it becomes the whole model.
explanation.student:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs, including LSTMs and GRUs) compute a hidden state for position $t$ from the state at $t-1$. This chain is inherently sequential, so the positions inside one training example cannot be processed in parallel, and memory limits how many examples can be batched at long sequence lengths.

Attention mechanisms already helped RNN translation models by letting the decoder look back at any input position. The paper's proposal is to drop recurrence entirely and build the model from **attention alone**, which makes every layer fully parallel across positions.
explanation.expert: Sequential computation in RNN encoder-decoders precludes intra-example parallelism and becomes the bottleneck at long sequence lengths; factorization tricks and conditional computation help but don't remove the constraint. Convolutional alternatives (ByteNet, ConvS2S) parallelize, yet the number of operations relating two distant positions grows linearly or logarithmically with distance. The Transformer relates any two positions in a constant number of operations, at the cost of averaging attention-weighted positions, which multi-head attention counteracts.

quotes.text: sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths
In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output.

beginner.question: Why were the older translation programs slow?
choices: They looked up every word in a dictionary
Each word had to wait for the word before it
beginner.why: They read one word after another, so word 10 had to wait for word 9.

beginner.question: What role does attention play in the Transformer?
choices: A small helper added to step-by-step reading
It is replaced by a running memory
beginner.why: Attention had been used as a helper before; here it becomes the whole model.

student.question: What stops an RNN from processing positions within one example in parallel?
choices: The state at $t$ depends on the state at $t-1$
Softmax must normalize the attention weights
student.why: Each hidden state is computed from the previous one, so the chain is inherently sequential.

student.question: What does the paper propose instead of recurrence?
choices: Adding attention on top of LSTMs
Building the model from attention alone
student.why: The Transformer drops recurrence entirely and relies on attention alone, making each layer fully parallel.

expert.question: How many operations does the Transformer need to relate two distant positions?
expert.why: Unlike ConvS2S (linear) or ByteNet (logarithmic), the Transformer relates any two positions in a constant number of operations.

expert.question: What cost of constant-operation relating does multi-head attention counteract?
expert.why: Relating positions in one step averages attention-weighted positions; multi-head attention counteracts this.

explanation.beginner:
The Transformer has two halves. The **encoder** reads the whole English sentence and turns each word into a list of numbers that captures its meaning in context. The **decoder** then writes the German sentence one word at a time, peeking at the encoder's notes and at the words it has already written.

Each half is a stack of 6 identical blocks, like floors in a building. Every floor refines the understanding a little more.
explanation.student:
Like earlier translation models, the Transformer is an encoder-decoder. The encoder maps the input tokens to a sequence of vectors; the decoder generates the output one token at a time, auto-regressively, feeding its previous outputs back in.

Both halves stack $N = 6$ identical layers. An encoder layer has a self-attention sub-layer and a feed-forward sub-layer [e3]; a decoder layer adds a third sub-layer that attends over the encoder's output. Each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization, and all vectors have size $d_{model} = 512$.
explanation.expert: Standard encoder-decoder with $N=6$ layers per side. Each sub-layer computes $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$, with all sub-layers and embeddings producing $d_{model}=512$ outputs to make the residuals work. Decoder self-attention is masked so position $i$ only sees positions $< i$, and output embeddings are offset by one, preserving the auto-regressive property. The decoder's middle sub-layer is encoder-decoder attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder output).

quotes.text: Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure.

beginner.question: What does the decoder do?
choices: Reads the whole English sentence at once
Writes the German sentence one word at a time
Adds a position stamp to each word
beginner.why: The decoder writes the output one word at a time, peeking at the encoder's notes and its own earlier words.

beginner.question: What does stacking identical blocks, like floors in a building, achieve?
choices: Each floor translates a different sentence
Only the top floor does real work
Each floor refines the understanding a little more
beginner.why: Each half stacks 6 identical blocks, and every floor refines the understanding a bit more.

student.question: What extra sub-layer does a decoder layer have compared with an encoder layer?
student.why: Decoder layers add a third sub-layer that attends over the encoder's output.

student.question: How is each sub-layer wrapped?
choices: Residual connection followed by layer normalization
student.why: Every sub-layer sits inside a residual connection followed by layer normalization.

expert.question: Why is decoder self-attention masked?
choices: To cut the cost of attention
So position $i$ only sees positions $< i$
To hide the encoder output from lower layers
expert.why: Masking, with outputs offset by one, keeps the decoder auto-regressive.

expert.question: In encoder-decoder attention, where do queries, keys and values come from?
choices: Queries from encoder; keys and values from decoder
Queries from decoder; keys and values from encoder output
expert.why: The decoder's middle sub-layer takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder output.

explanation.beginner:
Attention works a bit like a library search. Each word writes a **question** ("what am I looking for?"), and every word also carries a **label** ("here is what I am about") and some **content**. A word compares its question with every label; the better the match, the more of that word's content it takes in.

So in "the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired", the word "it" can learn to pay most attention to "animal". The recipe for this is equation [e1].
explanation.student:
Each position produces three vectors: a query $q$, a key $k$ and a value $v$. Stacking them for all positions gives matrices $Q$, $K$ and $V$. The output for each query is a weighted average of the values, where the weights come from how similar the query is to each key (their dot product), turned into probabilities with softmax [e1].

The dot products are divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$. Without this, large vectors give very large dot products, softmax becomes nearly all-or-nothing, and its gradients become tiny, which stalls learning.
explanation.expert: Attention is a mapping from a query and key-value pairs to a weighted sum of values. The paper uses dot-product (multiplicative) attention, computed for all queries at once as $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ [e1]. It is faster and more memory-efficient than additive attention thanks to optimized matrix multiplication. The $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling counters the variance growth of $q\cdot k$ (variance $d_k$ for unit-variance components), which otherwise drives softmax into saturated, small-gradient regions; without it, additive attention outperforms dot-product attention at larger $d_k$.

quotes.text: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

beginner.question: In the library analogy, what decides how much of another word's content a word takes in?
choices: How close together the two words sit
How well its question matches that word's label
How long the other word is
beginner.why: A word compares its question with every label; the better the match, the more content it takes in.

beginner.question: In "the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired", what can "it" learn to focus on?
beginner.why: Attention lets "it" pay most attention to "animal", the thing that was tired.

student.question: How are the attention weights computed?
student.why: Query-key dot products measure similarity and softmax turns them into probabilities that weight the values.

student.question: Why are dot products divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$?
choices: To make attention cheaper to compute
Large dot products make softmax all-or-nothing with tiny gradients
To give the values unit length
student.why: Without scaling, large dot products saturate softmax and its gradients shrink, stalling learning.

expert.question: Why use dot-product rather than additive attention?
choices: It wins at every $d_k$ even unscaled
It is faster and more memory-efficient via matrix multiplication
expert.why: Dot-product attention benefits from optimized matrix multiplication, making it faster and more memory-efficient.

expert.question: For unit-variance components, what is the variance of $q\cdot k$?
expert.why: The variance of $q\cdot k$ grows to $d_k$, which the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling counters.

explanation.beginner:
One round of attention can only focus on one kind of connection at a time. So the Transformer runs **8 attention rounds side by side**, called heads. One head might link pronouns to nouns, another might link verbs to their objects, another might track word order. Their results are glued together at the end [e2].

It's like asking eight friends to read the same sentence, each paying attention to something different, and then combining their notes.
explanation.student:
Instead of one attention over 512-dimensional vectors, the model projects $Q$, $K$ and $V$ into $h = 8$ smaller spaces (64 dimensions each) with learned matrices, runs attention in each, concatenates the 8 results and projects them back [e2]. The total cost is about the same as one full-size attention.

The point is that a single attention averages everything into one weighting, while separate heads can attend to **different kinds of information at different positions** at the same time.
explanation.expert: $h=8$ heads with $d_k=d_v=d_{model}/h=64$, each with its own projections $W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V$, outputs concatenated and projected by $W^O$ [e2]; reduced per-head dimension keeps total cost comparable to single-head full-dimensional attention. Multi-head attention is used three ways: encoder self-attention, masked decoder self-attention (illegal connections set to $-\infty$ before softmax), and encoder-decoder attention. Table 3 ablations show single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse, and too many heads also degrade quality.

quotes.text: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

beginner.question: Why run several attention heads instead of one?
choices: One round can only focus on one kind of connection
One round cannot read long sentences
More rounds make the model smaller
beginner.why: A single round of attention focuses on one kind of connection at a time, so 8 heads run side by side.

beginner.question: What happens to the heads' results at the end?
choices: Only the best head is kept
They are averaged into one number
beginner.why: Like combining eight friends' notes, the heads' results are glued together at the end.

student.question: How many dimensions does each head's projected space have?
student.why: The model projects into $h = 8$ smaller spaces of 64 dimensions each.

student.question: What can separate heads do that one attention cannot?
choices: Remove the need for positional encodings
Attend to different kinds of information at different positions
student.why: One attention averages everything into one weighting; separate heads attend to different information at once.

expert.question: In the Table 3 ablations, how did single-head attention compare?
expert.why: Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse, though too many heads also hurt quality.

expert.question: How are illegal connections handled in masked decoder self-attention?
expert.why: Illegal connections are set to $-\infty$ before softmax so they get zero weight.

explanation.beginner:
After attention, each word passes through a small calculator of its own [e3] that sharpens its meaning. This happens to every word separately.

There's one catch. Attention treats a sentence like a bag of words, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same. To fix this, the model adds a **position stamp** to each word, made from smooth waves of different lengths [e4]. Now every word knows where it sits, and the model can tell nearby words from far ones.
explanation.student:
Every layer also has a position-wise feed-forward network: two linear layers with a ReLU between them, applied to each position independently [e3]. The inner layer is wider ($d_{ff} = 2048$) than the model size (512).

Since attention has no notion of order, the model adds **positional encodings** to the input embeddings: sine and cosine waves whose wavelengths range from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ [e4]. The authors chose waves because the encoding of position $pos + k$ is a fixed linear function of the encoding at $pos$, which should make relative positions easy to learn. Learned position embeddings gave nearly identical results.
explanation.expert: FFN is two linear maps with ReLU, $d_{ff}=2048$, equivalently two kernel-size-1 convolutions [e3]. Input and output embeddings share weights with the pre-softmax projection, scaled by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$. Absolute sinusoidal positional encodings [e4] are summed with embeddings; for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$, the hypothesized benefit being easy learning of relative attention and extrapolation to longer sequences. Learned positional embeddings performed nearly identically (Table 3, row E).

quotes.text: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

beginner.question: Why does the model add a position stamp to each word?
choices: To make each word's numbers shorter
Attention alone treats a sentence like a bag of words
To mark which words are nouns
beginner.why: Without it, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same to attention.

beginner.question: What are the position stamps made from?
beginner.why: The stamps are built from smooth waves of different lengths, so each word knows where it sits.

student.question: What is the position-wise feed-forward network?
choices: Two linear layers with a ReLU, applied per position
An LSTM run over all positions
student.why: It is two linear layers with a ReLU between them, applied to each position independently.

student.question: Why did the authors choose sine and cosine waves?
choices: They are cheaper than learned embeddings
The encoding of $pos + k$ is a linear function of that at $pos$
student.why: This linear relation should make relative positions easy to learn; learned embeddings did nearly the same.

expert.question: The FFN is equivalent to what?
expert.why: Two linear maps applied per position equal two kernel-size-1 convolutions.

expert.question: How did learned positional embeddings compare with sinusoidal ones (Table 3, row E)?
expert.why: Learned positional embeddings performed nearly identically to the sinusoidal encoding.

explanation.beginner:
The authors compare their design with the older ones on three things: how much work each layer does, how much of that work can happen at the same time, and how many steps a signal needs to travel between two far-apart words.

Self-attention wins on the last two. Any word reaches any other word in **one step**, and all words are processed at once. The only cost is that every word looks at every other word, which gets expensive for very long texts.
explanation.student:
Section 4 compares self-attention, recurrent and convolutional layers on per-layer cost, parallelism (minimum sequential operations) and **maximum path length** between any two positions, since shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn.

A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequential steps, while an RNN needs $O(n)$. Its cost per layer is $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, cheaper than recurrence's $O(n \cdot d^2)$ whenever the sequence length $n$ is smaller than the vector size $d$, which is the usual case for sentences.
explanation.expert: Table 1: self-attention has $O(n^2 d)$ complexity, $O(1)$ sequential operations and $O(1)$ maximum path length, versus $O(nd^2)$, $O(n)$, $O(n)$ for recurrent and $O(knd^2)$, $O(1)$, $O(\log_k n)$ for dilated convolutions. Self-attention is faster than recurrence when $n < d$, typical of sub-word sentence representations; restricted self-attention over a neighbourhood $r$ trades path length $O(n/r)$ for cost on very long sequences. Attention heads also yield more interpretable models, with heads exhibiting syntactic and semantic behaviour.

quotes.text: The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network.

beginner.question: How many steps does a signal need to travel between any two words in self-attention?
choices: One step per word in between
beginner.why: Any word reaches any other word in one step.

beginner.question: What is the main cost of self-attention?
choices: Words can't be processed at the same time
Every word looks at every other word, costly for long texts
beginner.why: Since every word looks at every other word, it gets expensive for very long texts.

student.question: Why does a shorter maximum path length matter?
choices: It makes long-range dependencies easier to learn
It reduces the number of parameters
It removes the need for softmax
student.why: Shorter paths between positions make long-range dependencies easier to learn.

student.question: When is self-attention cheaper per layer than recurrence?
student.why: $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ beats $O(n \cdot d^2)$ when $n < d$, the usual case for sentences.

expert.question: What is the maximum path length for dilated convolutions with kernel width $k$?
expert.why: Table 1 lists $O(\log_k n)$ for dilated convolutions, versus $O(1)$ for self-attention.

expert.question: What does restricted self-attention over a neighbourhood $r$ trade?
expert.why: Restricting to a neighbourhood $r$ lengthens paths to $O(n/r)$ to save cost on very long sequences.

explanation.beginner:
The team trained the Transformer on millions of English-German and English-French sentence pairs, using 8 graphics cards. The biggest version trained for 3.5 days, which was far less computing than earlier record-holders needed.

The result: the best translation scores anyone had reported, for both language pairs. They also showed it could learn to break English sentences into their grammar parts, so it wasn't only good at translation.
explanation.student:
Models were trained on WMT 2014 English-German (about 4.5 million sentence pairs) and English-French (36 million) on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, using Adam with a learning rate that warms up and then decays [e5]. Dropout and label smoothing were used to regularize.

The big model scored **28.4 BLEU** on English-German, over 2 points above the previous best, including ensembles, and **41.8 BLEU** on English-French, at a fraction of the earlier training cost. It also did well on English constituency parsing with little task-specific tuning.
explanation.expert: Adam ($\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.98, \epsilon=10^{-9}$) with linear warm-up over 4000 steps then inverse-square-root decay [e5]; residual dropout $P_{drop}=0.1$, label smoothing $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$ (hurts perplexity, helps BLEU). Base model 100k steps (12 h), big model 300k steps (3.5 days) on 8 P100s. Transformer (big): 28.4 BLEU En-De, 41.8 En-Fr (with $P_{drop}=0.1$ for En-Fr), at $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ training FLOPs for En-De. A 4-layer model reaches 91.3 F1 on WSJ-only constituency parsing and 92.7 semi-supervised.

quotes.text: We trained on the standard WMT 2014 English-German dataset consisting of about 4.5 million sentence pairs.
outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU

beginner.question: How did the Transformer's translation scores compare with earlier programs?
choices: Best anyone had reported, for both language pairs
Good, but below the older models
beginner.why: It got the best translation scores anyone had reported for both language pairs.

beginner.question: What was the Transformer trained on?
choices: Millions of English-German and English-French sentence pairs
beginner.why: It learned from millions of sentence pairs in two language pairs.

student.question: How did the big model's English-German score compare with the previous best, including ensembles?
student.why: It scored 28.4 BLEU, over 2 points above the previous best, ensembles included.

student.question: Roughly how many sentence pairs were in WMT 2014 English-German?
student.why: English-German had about 4.5 million pairs; 36 million was English-French.

expert.question: What was the effect of label smoothing $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$?
expert.why: Label smoothing hurts perplexity but improves BLEU.

expert.question: By how much did Transformer (big) beat the best previous En-De result, ensembles included?
expert.why: 28.4 BLEU on En-De is more than 2.0 BLEU above the best previously reported models, including ensembles.

in_words.beginner: Compare every word's question with every word's label, turn the match scores into percentages, then mix the words' contents using those percentages.
in_words.student: Similarity scores between each query and every key (dot products), scaled down by $\sqrt{d_k}$ and normalized with softmax, become weights for averaging the value vectors.
in_words.expert: Batched dot-product attention with $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ temperature to keep logit variance near 1 and avoid softmax saturation.

symbols.meaning: queries: what each word is looking for
keys: what each word offers to be matched on
values: the content each word passes on
K flipped (transposed) so every query meets every key
length of each query and key vector (64)
turns scores into positive weights that add up to 1

in_words.beginner: Run attention 8 times, each with its own way of looking at the words, then glue the 8 answers together.
in_words.student: Each head projects Q, K and V into a smaller space with its own learned matrices and runs attention there; the heads' outputs are concatenated and mixed by one more matrix.
in_words.expert: h parallel attention functions over learned linear projections to $d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$, concatenated and projected by $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{model}}$.

symbols.meaning: number of heads (8)
the output of attention head number i
learned matrices that give head i its own view
learned matrix that mixes the heads back together
lay the heads' outputs side by side

in_words.beginner: Each word's numbers go through two simple calculation steps, with negative results set to zero in between.
in_words.student: Two linear layers with a ReLU in between, applied to every position separately with the same weights.
in_words.expert: Two affine maps with ReLU, $d_{model} \to d_{ff}=2048 \to d_{model}$, shared across positions, distinct per layer.

symbols.meaning: one word's vector coming out of attention
learned weight matrices
learned bias vectors
ReLU: keep positives, turn negatives into 0

in_words.beginner: Each position gets a unique pattern made of waves, some fast and some slow, like the hands of a clock. Adding it to a word tells the model where the word is.
in_words.student: Even dimensions use sine, odd ones cosine, each pair with a different wavelength, so every position gets a distinct, smoothly varying code that is added to the word embedding.
in_words.expert: Fixed sinusoids with geometrically spaced wavelengths from $2\pi$ to $10000\cdot2\pi$; $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$, easing relative-position attention.

symbols.meaning: the word's position in the sentence (0, 1, 2, ...)
which pair of dimensions of the vector
length of every word vector (512)
the position code added to the word

in_words.beginner: Training starts with small, careful steps, speeds up for a while, then slowly takes smaller steps again as the model gets better.
in_words.student: The learning rate grows linearly for the first 4000 training steps (warm-up), then shrinks in proportion to one over the square root of the step number.
in_words.expert: Linear warm-up for $warmup\_steps=4000$, then $\propto step^{-1/2}$ decay, scaled by $d_{model}^{-1/2}$.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: The Transformer - model architecture.

explanation.beginner: A map of the whole model. The left tower reads the sentence you start with, the right tower writes the translation one word at a time, and arrows show information moving between them.
explanation.student: The encoder (left) is a stack of N = 6 identical layers, each with self-attention and a feed-forward network. The decoder (right) adds a third block that attends to the encoder's output, and its self-attention is masked so it can't peek at future words.
explanation.expert: Encoder and decoder stacks of N = 6 layers; each sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The decoder's masked self-attention preserves the autoregressive property, and encoder-decoder attention draws keys and values from the encoder output. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings.

figures.how_to_read: Read from the bottom up: words enter at the bottom, pass through the stacked blocks (the "N×" means the block repeats 6 times), and the probabilities for the next word come out at the top right.
figures.takeaway: The whole model is built from attention and simple feed-forward layers, with no recurrence anywhere.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: (left) Scaled Dot-Product Attention.

explanation.beginner: Two diagrams of the attention step. On the left, one word asks a question of every other word and gets back a blend of their answers. On the right, that is done several times side by side and the results are joined.
explanation.student: Left: queries are compared with keys by a dot product, scaled, optionally masked, and put through a softmax; the weights then average the values. Right: multi-head attention runs h such attention layers in parallel on different learned projections and concatenates them.
explanation.expert: Left: softmax(QK^T/√d_k)V with an optional mask. Right: h = 8 heads, each with its own projections W^Q, W^K, W^V to d_k = d_v = 64, concatenated and projected by W^O.

figures.how_to_read: Each box is one operation and the arrows show the order, bottom to top. In the right diagram, the stacked shadows behind the middle box stand for the h heads running at once.
figures.takeaway: Multi-head attention is just scaled dot-product attention run several times in parallel.

concepts.meaning: Turning one sequence into another, like a sentence in English into one in German.
The half of the model that reads the input and turns it into numbers.
The half of the model that writes the output, one token at a time.
A way for each word to pull in information from the words most relevant to it.
Attention where a sentence's words attend to other words of the same sentence.
A function that turns any list of scores into positive weights adding up to 1.
A list of numbers that stands for a word, learned so similar words get similar lists.
Adding a layer's input to its output, which makes deep networks easier to train.
Rescaling a vector's numbers to a standard range so training stays stable.
A score from 0 to 100 for how closely a machine translation matches human ones.
Training the model to be slightly less than 100% sure, which helps it generalize.
Processing a sequence step by step, each step depending on the one before.

prepared_answers.question: Why do they divide by the square root of d_k?

parts.text: Without the scaling, the dot products between queries and keys get large when the vectors are long. Large scores push softmax into a region where almost all the weight goes to one word, and there its gradients are tiny, so the model learns very slowly.

citations.quote: To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by

parts.text: Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the scores in a moderate range, so softmax stays smooth and training keeps moving.

prepared_answers.question: How long did training take, and on what hardware?

parts.text: All models were trained on a single machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.

citations.quote: We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.

parts.text: The base model trained for 100,000 steps, about 12 hours. The big model trained for 300,000 steps, which took 3.5 days.

citations.quote: The big models were trained for 300,000 steps (3.5 days).

prepared_answers.question: Does the Transformer work for anything besides translation?

parts.text: Yes. The authors also tried English constituency parsing, which means breaking a sentence into its grammatical parts, and the Transformer did well both with lots of training data and with little.

citations.quote: We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

parts.text: They end by saying they plan to apply attention-based models to other tasks too.

citations.quote: We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks.
